claims.text: Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles possess short-range local chemical ordering.
Short-range local chemical ordering broadens the premelting regime of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Local chemical ordering stabilizes partial surface melts at lower temperatures.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles undergo a multi-step melting sequence before complete melting.
Single-element nanoparticle counterparts melt more abruptly than Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
The as-synthesized Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are single-phase.
The nanoparticles retain their single-phase state through rapid cooling from a previous high-temperature process.
Heating produces transient compositional heterogeneities with slightly different local elemental ratios near the particle surface.
The transient compositional heterogeneities reduce local free-energy barriers to melting.
Reduced local free-energy barriers cause surface melting to begin early and progress inward.
Chemical complexity and partial short-range order stabilize the molten surface layer.
Stabilization of the molten layer extends the premelting interval and delays complete molten collapse.
Relative to comparable single-metal or binary nanoparticles, Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles have a lower onset temperature for partial surface melting.
Relative to the baseline particles, Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles have a broader premelting region.
Multi-element entropic stabilization delays the final melting point of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles relative to the baseline.
Comparable pure-Ni or Fe–Ni nanoparticles display a sharper and more abrupt melting transition under the same thermal cycle.
The proposed mechanism applies to minimally oxidized Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles between 5 and 20 nm under heating rates below approximately 100 K/min.
Strong surface oxidation or extremely rapid heating or cooling can alter the premelting pathway.
